clue.text: Delete replacement document

parts.note: a sub is a replacement, the player sent on in another's place
a tract is a short written document, usually a pamphlet arguing a case

explanation.surface: A curt filing instruction: get rid of the document that replaced the old one.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here announces wordplay — no indicator, no link word — so the only warning that the last two words are pieces is that the first cannot fill eight squares. Both of them are nouns pretending to modify each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Subtract and delete share the take-away sense: something that was there is removed and not put back.

clue.text: Bare message delivered — take off a little weight

parts.note: to take off your clothes is to strip
the word itself, taken as a letter
a gram is a very small unit of weight

explanation.surface: A blunt piece of news someone has been handed: lose a bit of weight.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash does all the separating — everything before it defines, everything after is material. 'Take off' is the undressing sense, not departing or imitating.
explanation.definitionFit: A strippagram is a novelty greeting delivered in person by a performer who undresses while giving it, so the message really does arrive bare.

clue.text: Autocrat runs into serious difficulty

indicators.note: Something that goes into another thing ends up within it, so the letter named is planted inside the longer run rather than set beside it.

parts.note: a big bother is serious difficulty
r = runs on a cricket scorecard

explanation.surface: A newspaper line about a dictator sprinting headlong into trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs into' reads as one phrase and parses as two jobs: the runs are a letter, the into puts that letter somewhere. The pair of words wanted is the mildest possible way to say serious difficulty, which is why it hides.
explanation.definitionFit: Big Brother is the all-seeing ruler of Orwell's 1984, and his name has become the standard English shorthand for an absolute, watchful authority.

clue.text: One evaluating evidence of old volcano having blown its top

indicators.note: A thing that has blown its top has lost whatever sat at the very top of it, and in a down entry the top is the opening letter.

parts.note: the bowl an extinct volcano leaves behind is a crater

explanation.surface: An expert weighing up what is left of a mountain that erupted long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blown its top' is plain volcano talk in the surface and an instruction in the parse, which is the neatest kind of double duty. The word it acts on is never written down: you have to supply it from 'evidence of old volcano' first.
explanation.definitionFit: A rater is one who assigns a rating, putting a value on whatever is placed in front of them.

clue.text: Exceptionally strong cluing for grooming apparatus

indicators.note: Something exceptional departs from the usual, and letters departing from their usual order arrive rearranged.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

explanation.surface: A setter being congratulated on an unusually well-clued puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is a compliment about crosswords, so it reads as the setter's own comment rather than as raw material. Twelve letters is a long shuffle — count them against the enumeration before trusting it.
explanation.definitionFit: Curling tongs are the heated rods hair is wound round to put a wave in it, apparatus used for grooming.

clue.text: Commercial division is off course

parts.note: a commercial is an ad
a rift is a division, a split opened between people

explanation.surface: A company's commercial division heading the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial division' looks like a department on an org chart and is two unrelated pieces. Nothing marks the join, which is normal for a two-piece charade and is most of the difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat adrift has lost its heading and goes wherever the current takes it, which is being off course exactly.

clue.text: Daughter torn apart over mother returning has gone insane

indicators.note: Something returning comes back the way it went, so those letters are read from their far end.
In a down entry whatever is over something sits above it, so the pieces named first go on top of the piece named last.

parts.note: d = daughter in family trees and registers
riven means torn apart, split violently
a dam is an animal's mother, written back to front

explanation.surface: A family in pieces: the daughter distraught, the mother on her way home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dam' for mother comes from breeding — the female parent of a horse or a dog — and it is the three-letter mother crosswords always reach for. Forwards it spells a barrier, which is the joke in turning it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone driven mad has been pushed into insanity by something outside them: the same state as having gone insane, told from the other end.

clue.text: Electronic device lets assistant fill in papers

indicators.note: To fill something in is to put material into the space inside it, so the short piece lands in the middle of the other.

parts.note: your papers are your ID, the documents proving who you are
a PA is a personal assistant

explanation.surface: A gadget sold on the promise that it spares an assistant the paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: Both abbreviations are office shorthand rather than crossword-only conventions, which is why the sentence reads so smoothly. 'Papers' here is the sense used at a border post, not the one on the newsagent's counter.
explanation.definitionFit: An iPad is Apple's tablet computer, an electronic device on the plainest reading of the words.

clue.text: Trifles raise some jealousy Othello harbours

indicators.note: To raise something is to lift it, and in a down entry lifting the letters means reading them upwards from the bottom.
To harbour something is to shelter it out of sight, so the run of letters lies concealed within the words named.
Some of a thing is a part of it, so what is wanted is a run of letters inside the words rather than the words themselves.

parts.note: the run S-Y-O-T straddles the gap between the two words, and it is read the other way

explanation.surface: Othello nursing the jealousy his play is famous for.
explanation.walkthrough: Othello and jealousy belong together, so the two words sit side by side without drawing attention to the join they make. In a down clue 'raise' always means the buried run is read from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: Toys are trifles in the older sense — small things of no real worth, the sense still alive in 'toying with' an idea.

clue.text: Suitable branch for leader's most important assistant

parts.note: the right tool for a job is the suitable one
an arm of an organisation is one of its branches

explanation.surface: Choosing the appropriate department to supply a chief's deputy.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are ordinary senses standing in plain sight: the fitting choice, and a division of a company. The definition treats the answer as a body part and the wordplay never touches one.
explanation.definitionFit: Your right arm is the one you rely on, so a leader's right arm is the deputy they could not manage without.

clue.text: Significant woman causing marital irregularity

parts.note: a significant decision is a big one
Amy is a woman's name

explanation.surface: An important woman at the centre of a marriage scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woman' asking for a name rather than a synonym is a standard move, and which name is left for the letters to decide. Short ones repay learning: ADA, AMY, EVE and their kind turn up constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Bigamy is going through a second marriage while the first still stands — an irregularity in the marital sense, and an offence in law.

clue.text: Hardening quality shown by compiler doing fast job

definitions.note: The second definition reads the entry as two separate words describing a person at work, where the entry itself is an adjective; the setter is leaning on the pun rather than on a strict swap.
definitions.meaning: said of cement, glue or plaster that goes solid soon after it is mixed
a crossword compiler is a setter, so one working at speed is setting quickly

explanation.surface: A crossword compiler getting the whole puzzle written at speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compiler' is the setter's word for himself, and here he claims to work fast. The hyphen in the enumeration is the tell that two words are coming, one of which is the trade he has just named.
explanation.definitionFit: Quick-setting is what is said of cement or glue that hardens fast, and the same two words taken literally describe a compiler — a setter — setting quickly.

clue.text: Golden quality in perfect works of art

indicators.note: What is in something sits inside it, so the pieces named before go within the word named after.

parts.note: pure means perfect, unmixed with anything else
or is gold in heraldry, the tincture of a gold field
a quality of a person is a trait

explanation.surface: A golden quality running through a set of flawless works of art.
explanation.walkthrough: The host word is split after a single letter, which is why the seam is so hard to find — most insertions land nearer the middle. OR for gold is heraldry's word and one of the most-used three-letter tricks going.
explanation.definitionFit: Portraiture is the art of picturing people, named as a whole body of work rather than as one painting.

clue.text: African native died next to capital theatre

parts.note: the hippopotamus is native to African rivers
d = died, the abbreviation on a gravestone or in a family tree
Rome is the capital of Italy

explanation.surface: A news line about an African local who died beside the theatre in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Native' pushes you towards a person and delivers an animal, and 'capital' towards money before it settles on a city. British variety halls took this Greek name in their dozens, the London one among them.
explanation.definitionFit: A hippodrome was a Greek arena for horse racing, and Victorian Britain borrowed the word for its grand variety theatres, several of which still trade under it.

clue.text: Rough ganger said make it bigger

indicators.note: A rough version of something is not the tidy finished one, so the letters arrive out of their proper order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: A foreman's blunt order to scale the job up.
explanation.walkthrough: A ganger is the foreman of a gang of labourers, which is what makes the surface a building site rather than nonsense. 'Said' looks like a homophone signal and is four letters of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To aggrandise something is to make it greater — bigger in size, wealth or standing.

clue.text: Board work well together

definitions.meaning: what you do at the door of a bus, a train or an aircraft
of two people, to rub along without friction

explanation.surface: The members of a board pulling in the same direction.
explanation.walkthrough: Three words, two definitions and no wordplay at all — which is why 'Board' reads as the committee the second word belongs to. A clue this short is almost always doing this.
explanation.definitionFit: To get on a train is to board it, and two people who get on work well together: one phrasal verb, two senses that never meet.

clue.text: Doctor clings to a longing for the past

indicators.note: To doctor something is to tamper with it, and letters tampered with come out in a new arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A doctor who cannot let go of a longing for how things used to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' opens the clue as a person and works as a verb, and the capital letter gives nothing away since every clue starts with one. The fodder runs straight into the definition with no join to mark the change.
explanation.definitionFit: Nostalgic describes someone whose mood is a fond longing for a time now gone.

clue.text: Leaving party inside to spend some time outdoors

indicators.note: What is inside something sits within it, so the short word is planted in the middle of the longer one.

parts.note: going means leaving, on your way out
a camp is a party in the factional sense, as in the Labour camp

explanation.surface: Slipping out of the party indoors to get some air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' is the word to distrust: not a celebration but a faction, the sense in 'the government camp'. Everything after 'inside' is definition, with 'to' the only join.
explanation.definitionFit: To go camping is to sleep out under canvas for a few days, which is spending time outdoors in the plainest way there is.

clue.text: Dislikes top class interpretations

parts.note: A is the top grade or class, as in A-list and grade A
rival versions of a story are rival interpretations

explanation.surface: A critic who cannot stand the most highly rated readings of a text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top class' is a two-word way of writing a single letter, and it is the only piece of the clue not supplying a whole word. Definition and wordplay both sound like opinions about the same interpretations, which is what welds the sentence together.
explanation.definitionFit: An aversion is a settled dislike of something, and the plural matches the plural the clue asks for.

clue.text: Con artist, half repudiated, making comeback

indicators.note: Half of a word is one of its two equal parts, so five of the ten letters are taken and five left behind.
Something making a comeback returns the way it went, so the letters are read from the far end.

parts.note: the first half of REPUDIATED is REPUD, and it comes back the other way round

explanation.surface: A swindler partly disowned by his associates and now back in business.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after the first two words hides that the definition ends there and everything else is instruction. Which half is meant is never said — only one of the two halves turns into anything.
explanation.definitionFit: To dupe someone is to trick them, so a duper is one who makes a living at it: the con artist of the clue.

clue.text: Greatly stressed when trading ends badly

indicators.note: Something done badly comes out wrong, and letters that come out wrong are not in the order they were handed over in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.surface: A dealer watching the market close on a thoroughly bad day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ends badly' is the phrase the eye wants to take whole; the parse takes 'ends' as material and leaves 'badly' behind as the instruction. Trading floors and anxiety go together well enough that the two halves feel like one thought.
explanation.definitionFit: Angst-ridden means filled with anxiety, which is what being greatly stressed comes to.

clue.text: Insect found in central Crimea, Ghana and Angola

indicators.note: What is central sits at the middle, so from each name only the letter or two at its centre is taken.

parts.note: the middle two letters of CRIMEA
the middle letter of GHANA
the middle two letters of ANGOLA

explanation.surface: A bug reported from Crimea, Ghana and Angola alike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Central' governs all three names, not only the one it stands in front of — the two six-letter countries give two letters each and the five-letter one gives a single letter. 'Found in' looks like a hidden-word signal and is only a join.
explanation.definitionFit: The imago is the adult form an insect reaches once it has finished changing, the stage after larva and pupa.

clue.text: Watchers regularly become experts

indicators.note: Letters taken regularly are taken at a fixed interval, every other one rather than all of them.

parts.note: every second letter of WATCHERS, starting from the second

explanation.surface: Spectators who have watched so long they have turned into experts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' never says where to start, and here it is the second letter; the other run of four is no word at all. An eight-letter word yielding four is the usual shape of this device.
explanation.definitionFit: An ace is someone outstanding at what they do — a flying ace, an ace mechanic — so aces are experts.

clue.text: Bog has a very hot flow

parts.note: bog and lav are both British slang for the lavatory
the word itself, taken as a letter

explanation.surface: A patch of marshy ground with something scalding running through it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bog' is the lavatory in British slang, and that is the sense wanted — the marsh is the decoy. The single letter A does real work here while reading as nothing but an article.
explanation.definitionFit: Lava is molten rock pouring out of a volcano, about as hot as a flow can get.

clue.text: Linger in church — it can be transformative

definitions.note: The setter defines by description instead of synonym: the 'it' stands for the answer, and the clue says what the thing does rather than offering a word that could replace it.

indicators.note: What is in something sits within it, so the word named first goes inside the letters named after it.

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
to hang about somewhere is to linger there

explanation.surface: Loitering at the back of a church and coming out a different person.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash marks where the wordplay stops; everything after it describes the answer rather than naming it. 'Hang' is the hang-around sense, and CE is the two letters crosswords use for church above all others.
explanation.definitionFit: Change is the thing that turns one state into another, so a phrase about being transformative lands on it squarely.

clue.text: Fix a little pick-me-up and some Italian food

indicators.note: A little of a word is not all of it, so the last letter is dropped before what is left is used.

parts.note: to rig a match is to fix it
the word itself, taken as a letter
a pick-me-up is a tonic, docked of its final letter

explanation.surface: Sorting out a small reviving drink and something Italian to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix' reads as arranging the evening and means to rig. The curtailment is the clue's only instruction, and 'little' is the whole of the warning you get.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigatoni are short ridged pasta tubes, one of the standard Italian shapes: food, and Italian.

clue.text: Nick is small — of course

parts.note: s = small on a clothing label
natch is clipped slang for naturally, meaning of course

explanation.surface: An offhand remark that someone called Nick is on the short side.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on the first word is free — every clue starts with one — so it can be a man's name in the surface and a verb underneath. 'Natch' is dated slang worth learning, because those five letters come from nowhere else.
explanation.definitionFit: To snatch something is to grab it and go, which is to nick it in the British slang sense of stealing.

clue.text: Don't pay attention to my views on regime changes

definitions.text: Don't pay attention to my views
definitions.note: The answer says 'me' where the definition says 'my views'; disregarding what someone thinks is the everyday way of disregarding the person.

indicators.note: A change leaves a thing different from how it was, so the letters are handed back in a different arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: Someone playing down their own opinion of a change of government.
explanation.walkthrough: The eye reads 'regime changes' as one political phrase, and that is what keeps the instruction out of sight. The fodder starts a word earlier than it looks, at 'on'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignore me is the instruction to take no notice of what I say, which is what paying no attention to my views amounts to.
